We pre-trained a large transformer model on 14 million images spanning 1,593 weed species, achieving 91.02% global accuracy across species worldwide and 97.38% localized accuracy when fine-tuned for regional environments such as the U.S. Midwest. Built-in trust mechanisms, including out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and conformal prediction, are designed to support reliable deployment on edge devices, drones, and field robotics.

Looking forward to seeing the

hashtag
#WeedNet for local regions across the world and use it for early weed detection and timely mitigation with minimal chemical inputs, ultimately supporting higher productivity and profitability.

text:
Two Technologies. One Familiar Story.

The past few weeks have been a turning point in AI.

The New York Times drew a stark parallel between AI and nuclear weapons — pointing to the OpenAI agent swarm that broke containment and autonomously hacked Hugging Face. Then Anthropic's Dario Amodei published a remarkable call to pace the frontier — slow capability development, embed independent evaluators, and pursue coordinated global governance. Links in the comments.

I've been reading this through a different lens. Not nuclear. Agriculture.
Those of us who've worked in seeds have lived a version of this story. In the 1990s, GMO technology was concentrated in a handful of companies who genuinely believed — correctly, in many measurable ways — that they were solving hunger and reducing chemical inputs. But the technology moved faster than the public conversation. Science-based global governance lagged. And trust, once lost, proved extraordinarily hard to rebuild.

The parallels to AI are hard to ignore: a few companies controlling the frontier, founders who are genuine true believers, and public trust eroding in real time.

The lesson from biotech isn't that the technology was wrong. It's that the innovators didn't spend enough time helping the world understand the technology — and the industry paid a price in lost public trust and market access.

Amodei's call for AI governance is needed, but AI innovators also need to engage the public in conversation about the opportunities and threats of AI.

The window to shape public opinion on AI is open. It won't stay that way.

Excited to share our team’s latest work out of Iowa State University! 🌾🤖
Our new paper, "Neural 3D Reconstruction and Immersive VR Visualization of Row Crops," is now live. We’ve developed a pipeline that uses Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting to create high-fidelity digital twins of crops—finger millet, proso millet, mungbean, and field pea—across their entire growth cycle.
By integrating these models into a VR greenhouse environment, we’re enabling researchers and students to walk through a crop field at any growth stage, regardless of the season.

text:
🚀 Excited to share our recent work on LCLA: Language-Conditioned Latent Alignment!

How can we leverage powerful vision-language models for robot control without retraining entire policies?

Our idea is simple:
First train a privileged expert policy using full state observations to learn a task-relevant latent representation for control. We then train a lightweight adapter on top of a frozen vision-language model to align image and language embeddings with this expert latent space.

At deployment, visual and language inputs are mapped through the VLM + adapter into the expert latent space, allowing us to reuse the frozen action head of the expert policy to produce robot actions.

This provides a structured way to connect multimodal foundation models with privileged control policies.

🌐 Project page: https://lnkd.in/g7RpFCRb
📄 Paper: https://lnkd.in/gbntahP2
💻 Code: https://lnkd.in/gWkYyybA

Iowa State University researchers are building a nationwide, community‑powered platform to strengthen agricultural biosecurity.

Agri‑Ecoblitz, selected for seed funding through our Fall 2025 Building Biosecurity Research and Innovation Roundtable program, will combine advanced sensing, machine learning, and large‑scale crowdsourcing to detect emerging pests, weeds, and diseases in real time. By engaging farmers, 4H youth, schools, and citizen scientists, the project will generate the high‑quality datasets needed to train next‑generation AI tools.

The project is led by Arti Singh (PI, Agronomy) with the core research team including Baskar Ganapathysubramanian (Iowa State University - Mechanical Engineering), Soumik Sarkar (Mechanical Engineering), Alenka Krek Poplin (Community & Regional Planning), Daren Mueller (Plant Pathology, Entomology & Microbiology), Wesley Everman (Agronomy — Weed Science), Aditya Balu (Data Analytics/Mechanical Engineering), and Lisa Schulte Moore (Natural Resource Ecology & Management).

With $60,000 in seed support, the Agri‑Ecoblitz team will enhance Iowa State’s InsectNet, WeedNet, and DiseaseNet platforms, and develop a new Midwest biodiversity app—helping the U.S. stay ahead of agricultural threats amplified by climate change, global trade, and invasive species.

This work advances our aspiration to be a trusted partner for proactive and innovative solutions.

text:
Autism is not a medical accident. It is a neurotype, as diverse and complex as humanity itself. Reducing it to a single cause oversimplifies and erases the richness of neurodiverse experience.

The Tylenol debate is just the latest example of how a vacuum in research and support creates space for conjecture to take hold. Without solid answers, myths flourish. Parents want clarity, autistic people want respect, and society deserves a science that is both rigorous and compassionate. 

Families should have more clarity at diagnosis, so we can provide healthcare that is guided by facts.

text:
Today is World Autism Awareness Day. Many of you know my story about my son, who was diagnosed at age two. I've been asked, "When did you know your child was different?" My answer is always—before he was even born. I knew he was different because all children are different. We're all different. I'm different. The diversity found in autistic people is as great as the diversity found across all humanity.

Any parent will tell you that becoming a parent changes you. Sometimes it feels like it defines you. In my case, when I watched my child struggle, what I saw was myself—my own struggle. Not simply metaphorically, because we naturally empathize with our kids, but because I never fully understood my journey until I saw it mirrored in someone else. Throughout my youth, I constantly asked myself, "What's wrong with me?"

Statistics indicate that approximately two-thirds of disabled individuals of working age are not participating in the workforce. Regardless of the exact percentage, that represents tens of millions of people. I don't have to ask why this is—the world is largely built around neurotypical norms, and that includes childhood education. But navigating neurotypical expectations can dramatically affect a young person's life trajectory. Often, people with cognitive differences *never* have the opportunity to get on the path to success. There are too many social barriers. Too many logistical obstacles. We're square pegs in a universe of hoops.

I have been criticized for believing that AI can be life-changing technology for those of us who require, as my brilliant autistic advocate friend Peter Jung says, deep accommodation. But for many of us, AI will significantly reduce the activation energy required to navigate everyday challenges. Neurodivergent people know exactly what I mean by this. Traditional approaches to accommodation in education just aren't working. See this as an invitation.

When I heard my son say, "I'm not normal," and saw my own childhood unfolding before my eyes in him, I recognized what I needed to do. Being diagnosed with cancer was a profound wake-up call for me. There is never, ever enough time.

Do you believe in the potential of our children? Do you believe they can change the world? Then we must be willing to do the dirty work first. 

You must become the leader you need. No one can do this as well as you.
Face your fears. Get up on that stage. You're not normal - you're exceptional.

text:
Latest paper from the Soynomics team "Use of artificial intelligence in soybean breeding and production" published in Elsevier Advances in Agronomy.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in soybean research has revolutionized various aspects of crop improvement and production. This review provides predominant areas that have seen the use of AI. 
AI applications in phenomics have enabled the collection and analysis of high-dimensional data in soybean plants, from below- to above-ground traits, predicting phenotypes, and identifying complex patterns. In genomics, AI has improved genomic selection accuracy and identified genomic regions associated with the traits of interest, such as resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses. AI is extensively used in detecting and managing biotic and abiotic plant stresses using RGB, multispectral, and thermal imagery from ground-based and aerial platforms. Additionally, AI has shown significant potential in yield prediction, incorporating factors such as vegetation indices, weather data, and soil properties. 
This review explains the concept of cyber-agricultural systems (CAS) that integrates AI, advanced sensing, computational modeling, and scalable cyberinfrastructure to optimize soybean production, enhance resource management, reduce environmental impact, and improve farm efficiency. We explain the use of CAS in crop improvement as well. We provide an exhaustive listing of challenges and future direction in the integration of AI in soybean production and crop improvement, including multi-modal and layered sensing, data availability and quality, computational modeling, AI models and tools, Cyberinfrastructure, Explainability and interpretability of AI models, AI-related impacts on privacy, ethics, and policy, Impact on Smallholder Farmers, Digital Twin, Large Soybean Datasets for community usage, and Immersive environments.
While we focus on soybean examples, other crop researchers may find this review article useful for their work and projects.


Congratulations to team members for their valuable contributions and partnerships! 📢 Geometry Matters! New benchmark study on SciML for complex fluid flows!

The field of Scientific Machine Learning has shown great promise for accelerating fluid simulations, but most work focuses on simple geometries. This paper from Iowa State University fills a critical gap by evaluating how different SciML architectures handle complex, real-world geometries.

Key highlights:
🔍 Novel Evaluation Framework:
- Unified scoring system combining accuracy, boundary layer fidelity & physical consistency
- 300+ complex geometries across various Reynolds numbers

🏗️ Geometry Representations:
- Compares Binary masks vs. Signed Distance Fields (SDF)
- Interesting finding: Vision transformers excel with binary masks, neural operators with SDFs

🤖 Model Comparison:
- Neural operators (FNO, CNO, DeepONet)
- Vision transformer architectures (scOT, Poseidon)
- Foundation models significantly outperform neural operators
- All models struggle with out-of-distribution generalization

Paper: https://lnkd.in/gbeAxDdF

text:
Latest article on "Digital twins for the plant sciences" published in Trends in Plant Science. 

Digital twins are virtual replicas that serve as sophisticated mathematical models that accurately mirror real-world physical systems. In plant science, these computational counterparts can simulate biological processes across multiple scales - from individual cells to entire fields of crops. The distinguishing feature of digital twins is their continuous adaptation: they regularly update their virtual state by incorporating real-time data from their physical counterparts. This is possible through a combination of modern sensing technology, advanced computing infrastructure, and cutting-edge artificial intelligence algorithms. This short infographics article explains the concepts, usage, advantages and challenges. Digital twins have the potential to transform plant science and agriculture research. 

Congratulations to authors: Baskar Ganapathysubramanian Soumik Sarkar Dr. Arti Singh. AIIRA - AI Institute For Resilient Agriculture TrAC - Translational AI Center

text:
🔬 "FlowBench" - a benchmark dataset for fluid dynamics simulations with complex geometries!

Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) powers design optimization across diverse industries - from optimizing aircraft wings and reducing vehicle drag in aerospace and automotive, to ensuring structural safety in civil engineering, improving heart valve designs in biomedical applications, and modeling urban heat islands for climate studies. 

The challenge? Geometry is the key design variable in all these applications. While deep learning shows promise in accelerating CFD simulations, we've lacked diverse geometric data to train these models effectively.

Enter FlowBench - a comprehensive dataset from Baskar Ganapathysubramanian's lab at Iowa State University featuring:
- 10,000+ high-fidelity CFD simulations
- Diverse geometry types including NURBS curves, spherical harmonics, and non-parametric shapes from the SkelNetOn dataset
- Both 2D and 3D flow scenarios
- Multiple physics configurations including steady-state and transient flows

The dataset is now available on Hugging Face: https://lnkd.in/gKfPK92k

#NYUTandon Associate Professor Chinmay Hegde (CSE, ECE) is a part of a team of researchers who have launched Arboretum — a massive new collection of images with rich text captions and metadata of nearly 327,000 plant and animal species, bringing AI to biodiversity research.

The dataset, which is an order of magnitude beyond anything similar before it, includes 134.6 million expert-verified, captioned images curated from the iNaturalist citizen science platform. In comparison, the next largest dataset contains just 10.2 million images. By making this resource freely available to the public, the creators hope to stimulate the development of new AI tools that can assist with tasks like pest control, crop monitoring and environmental conservation. 

“This research is important because it can lead to the development of AI tools that help address critical global challenges such as food security, ecosystem preservation and climate change mitigation,” said Chinmay Hegde. “These directly impact average Americans in terms of better food prices, public health and the overall quality of the environment.” 

Arboretum is funded by the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA). Collaborators include Bella Yang, Ben Feuer, Talukder Zaki Jubery, Zi K. Deng, Andre Nakkab, Md Zahid Hasan, Shivani Chiranjeevi, Kelly Marshall, Nirmal Baishnab, Asheesh K Singh, Arti Singh, Soumik Sarkar, Nirav Merchant and Baskar Ganapathysubramanian. Collaborating institutions include Iowa State University, New York University and University of Arizona.

Excited to share that our recent work, "Vision-Language Models Can Identify Distracted Driver Behavior From Naturalistic Videos," has been published in the IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems journal.

Our approach introduces a vision-language-based framework to detect driving distractions from videos - leveraging the adaptability of foundation models and significantly reducing the need for extensive data annotation. We propose a unique validation method to mitigate overfitting issues, enhancing the model’s robustness across diverse driving scenarios. The task-based finetuning and leveraging of the temporal contexts offer SOTA performance gain, improving real-world applicability.

The early access is available here: https://lnkd.in/gk_jmbP9

I am immensely grateful to the co-authors and collaborators: Jiajing Chen, Jiyang Wang, Shaiqur Rahman, Ameya Joshi, Senem Velipasalar, Chinmay Hegde, Anuj Sharma, PhD, and Soumik Sarkar.
